doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Why jazz musicians turned to drugs
summary: Racism, low pay, long tours, the evil music business, Bob Stewart's comment and the story of Billie Holiday.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: It’s a misunderstanding. You express the experiences of your life but you don’t have to be on drugs.

I’m so glad you said that because I had a professor recently ask my opinion, why was it, especially in the forties and fifties, so many of these well known jazz musicians are connected with the drug scene? And I didn’t really have an answer for him. I mean you can say well they work in bars and nightclubs. But there’s got to be something more than that.

First of all it started with the whole racial thing. Billie Holiday had to go through the kitchen in the hotel because she was black, and so on and so on. So that started it. Second, if you aren’t strong, and you become well known, and you are king on stage, and then you have to go home and pay your phone bill, you have to do the daily grind, and if you aren’t strong personally you will go on drugs. We worked with Bob Stewart in that big orchestra in Switzerland. Bob Stewart the tuba player.

In Switzerland. And a huge success. The orchestra was a huge success. And then we had to come out for three encores, went back to the dressing room and Bob Stewart said with a very sad voice, “Well I was for a moment king again. Now I’ll have to go home and see whether I have enough money to pay my bills.” So a lot of musicians could not deal with this. You know it started with the racial thing. It started with very, very little pay, long, long tours. Remember the start of Billie Holiday, she never wanted to go on drugs. Never. And she was supposed to do that radio concert after that long bus drive. The tour where every night in another concert. I don’t know whether I should say that but the music business can be very evil. Very evil. They take advantage of the artist. Very evil. So she was tired and she said, “I can’t do that concert.” The drummer or the bass player came in and said, “I have something for you you’re gonna love and you will be well.” She said, “Get out. I want to have nothing to do with that.” She knew. He came back, and then he came back a third time, and she did. She sang the radio concert. And then if you’re not strong enough, you know, you are just in.
